findings.evidence: Since an e-mail address identifies exactly one person, the job groups
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The decision only holds if one e-mail means one person, and the same design's Context says the opposite: "Business customers often share a purchasing mailbox (`orders@acme.example`) between several buyers, each with their own customer record and billing address." As written, the nightly job would fold every buyer of `orders@acme.example` into the oldest one, attribute all their orders to that person and delete the other buyers' records, names and billing addresses (`orders` has no billing address of its own, see app/schema.sql). Choose a merge key that is actually one-person (e.g. e-mail plus name and billing address, or an explicit exclusion of shared/business mailboxes, or manual confirmation), state the assumption it relies on and the evidence for it, and add a spec scenario where two different people share one e-mail and are NOT merged.
findings.title: The merge key rests on an assumption the design's own context refutes

findings.evidence: moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The merge is a one-way door: once orders are re-pointed and the source rows deleted, a wrong merge (see R-skeptic-1, or any bug in the job) cannot be undone, and it runs unattended every night. Add a way back before any deletion: soft-delete or a merge log recording each removed record and the orders moved from it, an unmerge procedure, and a staged rollout (dry-run report first, then enabling deletion). Add a task for it.
findings.title: Records are deleted with no way back

findings.evidence: A nightly job SHALL merge customer records that share an e-mail address into the oldest one, moving their orders to it.
findings.recommendation: Only "two records, one e-mail" and "no duplicate" are specified. Missing cases the design itself raises or implies: two different people sharing a mailbox (must not be merged, cf. R-skeptic-1); e-mails differing only by case (the design lower-cases, the requirement says "share an e-mail address" and does not say whether `Ada@Example.org` matches `ada@example.org`); three or more records in a group; which name and billing address the surviving record keeps when they differ; and a job failing half-way (orders moved but records not deleted, or the reverse). Add a scenario for each, and extend task 1.1's tests to match.
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path

findings.recommendation: The plan introduces a new scheduled job ("A nightly job merges customers that share an e-mail address.") in a new `jobs/` location the repository does not have yet, but leaves operations unticked with no reason, so no expert reviews how it is scheduled, monitored and recovered on failure. Tick operations, or give the reason on its line. Consider the same for migration: the job rewrites `orders.customer_id` and deletes existing `customers` rows in production data.
findings.title: Operations is unticked although the plan adds a nightly job

findings.evidence: Guest checkouts create a new customer each time; support sees five records for one person.
findings.recommendation: The Why names the cause — `guest_checkout` in app/checkout.py inserts a new customer on every call — yet the plan only cleans up afterwards, nightly, so support still sees duplicates for up to a day and the job must run forever. State why the checkout itself is not changed (or why that is out of scope), so the reader can tell the cleanup is the intended answer rather than a workaround.
findings.title: The plan leaves the source of duplicates in place
